Algebra::Linear Equations.title: Change the starting amount or the rate
Algebra::Linear Equations.prompt: A separate worked model charges a fixed number of credits plus credits per hour. Compare one changed feature at a time: does the line move or become steeper?

frames.label: Start: 6 + 2h
frames.caption: The starting charge is 6 credits. Every additional hour adds 2 credits, so equal one-hour steps produce equal rises.

frames.label: Raise fixed charge
frames.caption: Only the fixed charge changes: C=10+2h. Each output is 4 credits higher, while the per-hour rise remains 2; the lines are parallel.

frames.label: Raise hourly rate
frames.caption: Keep the fixed charge at 10 and change the rate to 4 credits/hour. The starting point stays fixed, but each one-hour rise doubles.

Algebra::Linear Equations.takeaway: An intercept change shifts every output equally. A rate change alters the rise for each input step.

Algebra::Linear Equations.title: Does it state an equality?
Algebra::Linear Equations.prompt: Drag each complete mathematical statement or expression into the matching group. An expression has a value; an equation asserts that two expressions are equal.
Algebra::Linear Equations.explanation: 3x+7 and 4(x−2) are expressions. Adding an equals sign and another expression creates an equation, as in 3x+7=19 and 4(x−2)=0. A variable alone does not make an expression an equation, and an equation need not already be solved.

Algebra::Linear Equations.title: Move a line, one setting at a time
Algebra::Linear Equations.prompt: Predict what changing a will do. Move its slider, then change only b. Compare your function with the dashed reference.

Advanced Math::Quadratics (Part 1).title: Track the vertex and zeros separately
Advanced Math::Quadratics (Part 1).prompt: Compare three fresh quadratics. Keep track of what stays fixed when one parameter changes; these are worked illustrations rather than the lesson’s practice questions.

frames.label: Start: vertex (1, −4)
frames.caption: The vertex is (1,−4), and the real zeros are −1 and 3. Vertex form identifies both the horizontal location and the minimum output.

stimulus.title: q(x)=(x−1)²-4
stimulus.note: Exact integer samples are joined for orientation; the formula defines the smooth parabola between them.

frames.label: Move up 3
frames.caption: Changing only the outside constant moves the vertex up to (1,−1). The zeros become 0 and 2; a vertical shift does not preserve zero locations.

stimulus.title: q(x)=(x−1)²-1
stimulus.note: Exact integer samples are joined for orientation; the formula defines the smooth parabola between them.

frames.label: Move right 2
frames.caption: Keep the minimum output −1 and replace the center 1 by 3. The whole graph moves right 2, including the zeros, now 2 and 4.

stimulus.title: q(x)=(x−3)²-1
stimulus.note: Exact integer samples are joined for orientation; the formula defines the smooth parabola between them.

Advanced Math::Quadratics (Part 1).takeaway: An outside shift changes heights and can change zeros. An inside shift moves every input location, including the vertex and zeros.

Advanced Math::Quadratics (Part 1).title: Reshape the quadratic
Advanced Math::Quadratics (Part 1).prompt: Predict what changing a will do. Move its slider, then change only b. Compare your function with the dashed reference.

Geometry & Trigonometry::Circles.title: Slide a chord away from the center
Geometry & Trigonometry::Circles.prompt: The circle’s radius stays 10 units. Compare three vertical lines and predict whether moving farther from the center lengthens or shortens the chord.

frames.label: x = 0
frames.caption: The diameter lies through the center: endpoints (0,−10) and (0,10), giving length 20.

stimulus.title: Circle x²+y²=100 with a vertical chord
stimulus.note: Boundary coordinates are rounded to six decimals and joined to approximate the circle. Chord endpoints and dimensions are exact.

frames.label: x = 6
frames.caption: Move the line to x=6 while keeping radius 10. The equation 6²+y²=100 gives endpoints y=±8, so the chord length is 16.

stimulus.title: Circle x²+y²=100 with a vertical chord
stimulus.note: Boundary coordinates are rounded to six decimals and joined to approximate the circle. Chord endpoints and dimensions are exact.

frames.label: x = 8
frames.caption: Move it farther to x=8. The equation 8²+y²=100 gives endpoints y=±6 and chord length 12; the radius has not changed.

stimulus.title: Circle x²+y²=100 with a vertical chord
stimulus.note: Boundary coordinates are rounded to six decimals and joined to approximate the circle. Chord endpoints and dimensions are exact.

Geometry & Trigonometry::Circles.takeaway: Chord length is 2√(r²−a²). With radius fixed, increasing the distance |a| from the center shortens the chord.

Geometry & Trigonometry::Circles.title: Does the point satisfy the circle equation?
Geometry & Trigonometry::Circles.prompt: For the circle x²+y²=100, drag each exact coordinate pair into on the circle or not on the circle. Being inside the circle does not mean lying on its boundary.
Geometry & Trigonometry::Circles.explanation: The on-circle points satisfy 6²+8²=100 and 0²+10²=100. The point (6,6) gives 72, so it lies inside rather than on the circle. The point (10,10) gives 200 and lies outside. Radius 10 means squared distance 100, not distance 100.

Algebra & Functions::Lesson 4 — Function.title: Swap the order of two functions
Algebra & Functions::Lesson 4 — Function.prompt: Use the fresh rules f(x)=3x−1 and g(x)=x+4. Follow the same inputs through the two orders, keeping the intermediate output visible.

frames.label: Read both rules
frames.caption: These outputs show the individual assignments before any composition. A function’s output can become the other function’s next input.

frames.label: f first, then g
frames.caption: The first stage produces f(x), and g adds 4 to that result. Thus g(f(x))=3x+3; the original input is not fed into g again.

frames.label: g first, then f
frames.caption: Now f multiplies the added 4 by 3 before subtracting 1. The result is f(g(x))=3x+11, eight more than the reverse order at every listed input.

Algebra & Functions::Lesson 4 — Function.takeaway: Composition order determines the intermediate input. Applying the same two rules in reverse order need not produce the same function.

Algebra & Functions::Lesson 4 — Function.title: Which inputs are in the real domain?
Algebra & Functions::Lesson 4 — Function.prompt: Use h(x)=√(x−2) as a real-valued function. Drag each proposed input into the allowed or excluded group. Zero is an allowed square-root output.
Algebra & Functions::Lesson 4 — Function.explanation: The radicand must satisfy x−2≥0, so x≥2. At x=2 the output is 0, and at x=6 it is 2; both are real. Inputs 1 and 0 give negative radicands. The restriction is on the original input before applying the square root.

Number & Quantity::Lesson 1 — Number Pro.title: Watch the percentage base change
Number & Quantity::Lesson 1 — Number Pro.prompt: A hypothetical quantity begins at 100 units, rises by 20%, then falls by 20%. Before changing frames, predict whether the final value returns to 100.

frames.label: Initial quantity
frames.caption: Percent changes need a base. At the start, 20% of 100 would be 20 units.

frames.label: After the increase
frames.caption: Multiply 100 by 1.20 to get 120. The next decrease uses this new base, so 20% now means 24 units rather than 20.

frames.label: After the decrease
frames.caption: Multiply 120 by 0.80 to get 96. Equal percentage changes in opposite directions do not cancel because their bases differ.

stimulus.title: Second change
stimulus.note: Combined multiplier: 1.20×0.80=0.96. This is a 4% decrease relative to the original 100.

Number & Quantity::Lesson 1 — Number Pro.takeaway: Apply each percentage to the current quantity. Opposite changes of the same rate combine to 1−r², not 1.

Precalc: Exponential and Logarithmic Fun.title: Find the ratio after removing the shift
Precalc: Exponential and Logarithmic Fun.prompt: Only the vertical shift c changes in f(x)=2·2^x+c. Compare raw outputs with outputs adjusted by the known shift.

frames.label: Shift c = 0
frames.caption: With no vertical shift, the raw outputs double at every one-unit input step. The constant ratio is 2.

stimulus.title: f(x)=2·2^x+(0)
stimulus.note: The exponential multiplier stays 2. A raw ratio involving a zero denominator cannot be calculated.

frames.label: Shift c = 5
frames.caption: Adding 5 leaves each adjusted value f(x)−5 unchanged from the base exponential. Raw ratios are no longer constant because the same 5 is added, not multiplied.

stimulus.title: f(x)=2·2^x+(5)
stimulus.note: The exponential multiplier stays 2. A raw ratio involving a zero denominator cannot be calculated.

frames.label: Shift c = -2
frames.caption: Subtracting 2 makes f(0)=0, so the first raw ratio is undefined. Adjusting by the known shift still recovers positive values 2,4,8,16 and constant ratio 2.

stimulus.title: f(x)=2·2^x+(-2)
stimulus.note: The exponential multiplier stays 2. A raw ratio involving a zero denominator cannot be calculated.

Precalc: Exponential and Logarithmic Fun.takeaway: Constant ratios apply to the exponential component. Remove a known vertical shift before using ratios to identify its multiplier.

Precalc: Exponential and Logarithmic Fun.title: What stays constant between steps?
Precalc: Exponential and Logarithmic Fun.prompt: Each card lists consecutive outputs at equally spaced inputs. Classify the displayed pattern by its constant nonzero difference or its constant positive ratio. Treat these as stated model patterns, not proof of how an unknown sequence continues.
Precalc: Exponential and Logarithmic Fun.explanation: The first two lists have differences +3 and −2, respectively. The last two have ratios 2 and 1/2. Their successive differences are not constant. Equal input spacing matters: a ratio across two input steps would be the square of the one-step multiplier, not automatically that multiplier itself.

Precalc: Exponential and Logarithmic Fun.title: Compare raw and shifted growth
Precalc: Exponential and Logarithmic Fun.prompt: Predict what changing a will do. Move its slider, then change only b. Compare your function with the dashed reference.

Precalc: Trigonometric and Polar Functio.title: Change height and timing independently
Precalc: Trigonometric and Polar Functio.prompt: The midline is fixed at 8 units. Compare the effect of doubling amplitude with halving period; only one parameter changes at each step.

frames.label: Amplitude 2, period 8
frames.caption: The midline stays at 8. A two-unit amplitude gives maximum 10 and minimum 6, and one cycle takes 8 hours.

stimulus.title: s(t)=8+2sin(2πt/8)
stimulus.note: Exact quarter-cycle key points are joined for orientation; the actual sinusoid is smooth between them. The axes stay fixed across frames.

frames.label: Amplitude 4, period 8
frames.caption: Only amplitude doubles: maxima and minima move to 12 and 4, while the peak and trough times stay fixed.

stimulus.title: s(t)=8+4sin(2πt/8)
stimulus.note: Exact quarter-cycle key points are joined for orientation; the actual sinusoid is smooth between them. The axes stay fixed across frames.

frames.label: Amplitude 4, period 4
frames.caption: Only the period halves. Maxima and minima keep the same heights, but two full cycles now fit into the same 8-hour window.

stimulus.title: s(t)=8+4sin(2πt/4)
stimulus.note: Exact quarter-cycle key points are joined for orientation; the actual sinusoid is smooth between them. The axes stay fixed across frames.

Precalc: Trigonometric and Polar Functio.takeaway: Amplitude changes the distance from the midline. Period changes how long a cycle takes, without changing its extreme heights.

Calc AB: Differentiation: Definition & F.title: Let a secant approach a tangent
Calc AB: Differentiation: Definition & F.prompt: Use the separate example f(x)=x² at input 1. Keep one point fixed and bring the second closer; compare a rate across an interval with the limiting rate.

frames.label: h = 1
frames.caption: The two points are (1,1) and (2,4). Their secant slope is 2+h=3; as h shrinks, it approaches the tangent slope 2.

stimulus.title: Secants to f(x)=x² at x=1
stimulus.note: The smooth parabola is approximated by joined samples. The secant and tangent segments are exact straight lines; h is nonzero in every frame.

frames.label: h = 0.5
frames.caption: The two points are (1,1) and (1.5,2.25). Their secant slope is 2+h=2.5; as h shrinks, it approaches the tangent slope 2.

stimulus.title: Secants to f(x)=x² at x=1
stimulus.note: The smooth parabola is approximated by joined samples. The secant and tangent segments are exact straight lines; h is nonzero in every frame.

frames.label: h = 0.1
frames.caption: The two points are (1,1) and (1.1,1.21). Their secant slope is 2+h=2.1; as h shrinks, it approaches the tangent slope 2.

stimulus.title: Secants to f(x)=x² at x=1
stimulus.note: The smooth parabola is approximated by joined samples. The secant and tangent segments are exact straight lines; h is nonzero in every frame.

Calc AB: Differentiation: Definition & F.takeaway: The derivative is the limit of secant slopes, not a substitution of h=0 into an undefined difference quotient.

Calc AB: Integration & Accumulation of C.title: Keep the partition; change the sampling method
Calc AB: Integration & Accumulation of C.prompt: A constructed rate is exactly r(t)=1+t liters/minute on 0≤t≤4. Keep two equal intervals [0,2] and [2,4] and compare the accumulated change.

frames.label: Left endpoints
frames.caption: The two widths are 2 minutes. Left heights 1 and 3 liters/minute give 2·1+2·3=8 liters, an underestimate because the true rate increases.

stimulus.title: Left sum for r(t)=1+t
stimulus.note: Accumulated change estimate: 8 liters. Vertical joins mark step boundaries, not additional flow. The integrand is a rate, so multiply by interval width.

frames.label: Right endpoints
frames.caption: Use right heights 3 and 5 instead, keeping the same partition. The sum becomes 2·3+2·5=16 liters, an overestimate.

stimulus.title: Right sum for r(t)=1+t
stimulus.note: Accumulated change estimate: 16 liters. Vertical joins mark step boundaries, not additional flow. The integrand is a rate, so multiply by interval width.

frames.label: Join endpoint heights
frames.caption: Average the endpoint heights on each interval: 2(1+3)/2+2(3+5)/2=12 liters. This is exact here because the stated rate is linear.

stimulus.title: Trapezoids for r(t)=1+t
stimulus.note: Accumulated change estimate: 12 liters. Vertical joins mark step boundaries, not additional flow. The integrand is a rate, so multiply by interval width.

Calc AB: Integration & Accumulation of C.takeaway: Signed height times width accumulates change. Exactness of trapezoids here comes from the stated linear rate, not from a table alone.

Calc BC: Parametric, Polar & Vector Func.title: Distinguish the region from the tracing count
Calc BC: Parametric, Polar & Vector Func.prompt: For the fresh polar example r=3, only the angle interval changes. Before moving to two turns, predict whether a doubled tracing interval creates a larger geometric disk.

frames.label: Half turn
frames.caption: A half-turn traces the upper semicircle once. The swept area is (1/2)·3²·π=9π/2 square units.

stimulus.title: Polar curve r=3, angle from 0 to π
stimulus.note: Radius is 3 throughout. Joined samples approximate the circular arc. A repeated trace overlaps itself, so its multiplicity cannot be read from the final outline alone.

frames.label: One full turn
frames.caption: The same radius traces the full disk once. Swept area is 9π square units, equal to the disk’s geometric area.

stimulus.title: Polar curve r=3, angle from 0 to 2π
stimulus.note: Radius is 3 throughout. Joined samples approximate the circular arc. A repeated trace overlaps itself, so its multiplicity cannot be read from the final outline alone.

frames.label: Two full turns
frames.caption: The visible boundary is unchanged, but the same disk is traced twice. The integral counts 18π square units, while the geometric union is still only 9π.

stimulus.title: Polar curve r=3, angle from 0 to 4π
stimulus.note: Radius is 3 throughout. Joined samples approximate the circular arc. A repeated trace overlaps itself, so its multiplicity cannot be read from the final outline alone.

Calc BC: Parametric, Polar & Vector Func.takeaway: The polar area integral accumulates swept area over the stated interval. Repeated tracing can count the same region more than once.

Stats: Inference for Categorical Data: P.title: Increase the sample size, keep the estimate
Stats: Inference for Categorical Data: P.prompt: Compare hypothetical samples with the same observed 60% success rate. What happens to uncertainty when the sample size is multiplied by four?

frames.label: n = 100
frames.caption: Keep the observed proportion at 0.60 and use the same 95% normal-interval method. The standard error is √(0.60·0.40/100)≈0.048990; the margin is 1.96 times that value.

stimulus.title: Constructed sample: 60 successes in 100
stimulus.note: Assume separate appropriate random samples and independence conditions for each hypothetical size; for sampling without replacement, each population is at least ten times its sample size. All observed success/failure counts exceed 10. Values are rounded only for display.

frames.label: n = 400
frames.caption: Keep the observed proportion at 0.60 and use the same 95% normal-interval method. The standard error is √(0.60·0.40/400)≈0.024495; the margin is 1.96 times that value.

stimulus.title: Constructed sample: 240 successes in 400
stimulus.note: Assume separate appropriate random samples and independence conditions for each hypothetical size; for sampling without replacement, each population is at least ten times its sample size. All observed success/failure counts exceed 10. Values are rounded only for display.

frames.label: n = 1600
frames.caption: Keep the observed proportion at 0.60 and use the same 95% normal-interval method. The standard error is √(0.60·0.40/1600)≈0.012247; the margin is 1.96 times that value.

stimulus.title: Constructed sample: 960 successes in 1600
stimulus.note: Assume separate appropriate random samples and independence conditions for each hypothetical size; for sampling without replacement, each population is at least ten times its sample size. All observed success/failure counts exceed 10. Values are rounded only for display.

Stats: Inference for Categorical Data: P.takeaway: At fixed confidence and sample proportion, quadrupling sample size halves standard error and margin. It does not remove bias or guarantee a representative realized sample.

Stats: Regression Analysis::5.1 Scatterp.title: Separate slope units from correlation
Stats: Regression Analysis::5.1 Scatterp.prompt: Use four fresh constructed pairs. Compare a change in response units with a simple response shift; the last frame returns to the original scale before adding 10.

frames.label: Original response units
frames.caption: The least-squares line is y-hat=0.5+0.6x. Correlation is 3/√10≈0.948683; it measures standardized linear association, not slope units.

stimulus.title: Constructed paired observations
stimulus.note: The response units/offset change, but the displayed axis ranges stay fixed so the numerical changes remain visible. Use the reported slope and invariant correlation. These observational illustrations make no causal claim.

frames.label: Multiply y by 10
frames.caption: Only the response unit scale changes. The fitted line becomes y-hat=5+6x: slope and residual magnitudes multiply by 10, while correlation stays unchanged.

stimulus.title: Constructed paired observations
stimulus.note: The response units/offset change, but the displayed axis ranges stay fixed so the numerical changes remain visible. Use the reported slope and invariant correlation. These observational illustrations make no causal claim.

frames.label: Add 10 to original y
frames.caption: Start again with the original scale and add 10 to every response. The line becomes y-hat=10.5+0.6x; slope, residuals and correlation are unchanged.

stimulus.title: Constructed paired observations
stimulus.note: The response units/offset change, but the displayed axis ranges stay fixed so the numerical changes remain visible. Use the reported slope and invariant correlation. These observational illustrations make no causal claim.

Stats: Regression Analysis::5.1 Scatterp.takeaway: Positive rescaling changes slope units but not correlation. Adding a constant changes the intercept while preserving slope, residuals and correlation.

Physics 1: Oscillations::7.2 Energy, pha.title: Follow the energy, not just the motion
Physics 1: Oscillations::7.2 Energy, pha.prompt: Explore a hypothetical ideal horizontal spring: k = 8 N/m, mass = 2 kg, amplitude = 1 m. Total energy is 4 J. Lines join calculated sample points; the dot marks spring potential energy at the selected position.

frames.label: Left turn
frames.caption: At x = −1 m: U = 4 J, K = 0 J and speed = 0. The restoring acceleration points right.

frames.label: Equilibrium
frames.caption: At x = 0 m: U = 0 J, K = 4 J and speed = 2 m/s. Direction of travel is not determined by energy alone.

frames.label: Half amplitude
frames.caption: At x = +0.5 m: U = 1 J and K = 3 J. Half the amplitude does not mean half the potential energy.

Physics 1: Oscillations::7.2 Energy, pha.takeaway: U + K stays 4 J. The horizontal axis is position, not time; identical energy at a position does not specify the direction of travel.

Physics 1: Linear Momentum::4.1 Momentum.title: Turn a force pulse into a velocity change
Physics 1: Linear Momentum::4.1 Momentum.prompt: A hypothetical 2 kg cart starts with velocity +2 m/s. Its net horizontal force is the triangular pulse shown; take right as positive. Move from force to impulse to momentum.

frames.label: Force pulse
frames.caption: The triangle has base 3 s and height 4 N. Its signed area is +6 N·s, not peak force × duration.

frames.label: Area builds
frames.caption: By 1.5 s the accumulated impulse is +3 N·s; by 3 s it is +6 N·s. These exact selected values summarize area, not force height.

frames.label: Momentum changes
frames.caption: Initial momentum is +4 kg·m/s. Adding +6 N·s gives +10 kg·m/s and final velocity +5 m/s.

Physics 1: Linear Momentum::4.1 Momentum.takeaway: Force–time area gives a change in momentum. Add the initial signed momentum before dividing by mass.

Physics 1: Fluids::8.2 Buoyancy, floatin.title: Watch support transfer to the water
Physics 1: Fluids::8.2 Buoyancy, floatin.prompt: A hypothetical solid object weighs 60 N and has total volume 0.006 m³. A force gauge supports it at rest while progressively more volume enters water. Use density 1,000 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s²; ignore air buoyancy.

frames.label: One-third immersed
frames.caption: Water supports 20 N; the gauge supplies the remaining 40 N.

stimulus.title: Static upward support and downward weight

frames.label: Two-thirds immersed
frames.caption: Water support rises to 40 N and gauge tension falls to 20 N.

stimulus.title: Static upward support and downward weight

frames.label: Fully immersed
frames.caption: Buoyancy equals the 60 N weight. In this ideal case the object is neutrally buoyant and gauge tension is zero.

stimulus.title: Static upward support and downward weight

Physics 1: Fluids::8.2 Buoyancy, floatin.takeaway: Buoyancy depends on displaced fluid volume. Weight stays 60 N throughout; the gauge reading changes because another force shares the support.

APES: Land and Water Use::5.3 Water with.title: Less withdrawal can mean less return flow
APES: Land and Water Use::5.3 Water with.prompt: In this hypothetical basin, crop consumption remains 36 million liters per day. All water not consumed returns promptly to the same usable source; ignore other flows. Efficiency here means crop consumption divided by withdrawal.

frames.label: 40% efficiency
frames.caption: Withdraw 90 ML/day: 36 is consumed and 54 returns. Net basin consumption is 36 ML/day.

stimulus.title: Daily water account — all values ML/day

frames.label: 60% efficiency
frames.caption: Withdraw 60 ML/day: the same 36 is consumed and 24 returns. Withdrawals fall by 30, but so do return flows.

stimulus.title: Daily water account — all values ML/day

frames.label: Compare changes
frames.caption: Withdrawal savings and basin-consumption savings are different quantities in the stated model.

APES: Land and Water Use::5.3 Water with.takeaway: Under these explicit return-flow assumptions, efficiency reduces withdrawal but not net consumption. Real return-flow location, timing and quality must be evaluated.

APES: Land and Water Use::5.3 Water with.title: Removal or consumptive use?
APES: Land and Water Use::5.3 Water with.prompt: Classify the quantity described, not the eventual fate of every drop. In this teaching model, consumed water does not return to the same usable source during the accounting period.

buckets.label: Withdrawal: water removed from a source
Consumption: water not returned to that source

items.text: Volume passing the river intake as a farm removes water, before accounting for any return flow.
Volume pumped out of an aquifer, measured at the pump outlet.
Water transferred to the atmosphere through crop evapotranspiration during the accounting period.
Water incorporated into harvested produce and carried out of the basin during the accounting period.

APES: Land and Water Use::5.3 Water with.explanation: Withdrawal measures removal at the source. Consumption is the part unavailable as same-source return during the specified period. They are related accounting quantities, not two sets of permanently different water molecules; some withdrawn water can return, while some is consumed.

APES: Populations::3.1 Population growth.title: Compare growth with and without a density limit
APES: Populations::3.1 Population growth.prompt: These are calculated teaching models, not observations. Start N = 100, r = 0.5 per step and K = 800. Update once each step: unlimited model N_next = 1.5N; density-limited model N_next = N + 0.5N(1 − N/800). Values are rounded only for display.

frames.label: First update
frames.caption: At step 1, unlimited N = 150.00; density-limited N = 143.75. Both use the same initial population and nominal r.

frames.label: Limits become visible
frames.caption: At step 3, unlimited N = 337.50; density-limited N = 278.38. Both use the same initial population and nominal r.

frames.label: Different trajectories
frames.caption: At step 5, unlimited N = 759.38; density-limited N = 468.54. Both use the same initial population and nominal r.

APES: Populations::3.1 Population growth.takeaway: Density dependence slows this model as N approaches K. These discrete illustrative updates are not measurements or a guarantee that real populations approach a fixed carrying capacity smoothly.

APES: The Living World: Ecosystems::1.3.title: Track nitrogen through distinct transformations
APES: The Living World: Ecosystems::1.3.prompt: Follow nitrogen forms in a simplified process diagram. Each frame isolates one pathway; these pathways can occur in different organisms and conditions, not as one mandatory linear trip for every nitrogen atom.

frames.label: Fixation
frames.caption: Nitrogen fixation changes atmospheric nitrogen into biologically usable reduced nitrogen; it is not nitrification.

stimulus.title: One entry pathway

steps.title: Atmosphere
steps.text: N₂

steps.title: Nitrogen fixation
steps.text: Certain microbes convert N₂ into ammonia/ammonium forms.

steps.title: Available reduced nitrogen
steps.text: NH₃ / NH₄⁺, depending on conditions

stimulus.note: Simplified pathway; organisms and conditions determine actual rates.

frames.label: Nitrification + uptake
frames.caption: Nitrification changes chemical form; assimilation incorporates inorganic nitrogen into biomass.

stimulus.title: From ammonium toward biomass

steps.title: Ammonium
steps.text: NH₄⁺

steps.title: Nitrification
steps.text: Microbial oxidation through nitrite (NO₂⁻) to nitrate (NO₃⁻).

steps.title: Assimilation
steps.text: Producers take up suitable inorganic nitrogen and incorporate it into organic molecules.

stimulus.note: Plants can use ammonium as well as nitrate; this diagram is one possible route.

frames.label: Return to atmosphere
frames.caption: Denitrification is a different microbial process from decomposition or fixation.

stimulus.title: One nitrogen return pathway

steps.title: Nitrate
steps.text: NO₃⁻ in a suitable environment

steps.title: Denitrification
steps.text: Microbial reduction under low-oxygen conditions can produce N₂.

steps.title: Atmosphere
steps.text: N₂ returns to the atmospheric reservoir.

stimulus.note: A simplified route; intermediates and gaseous products can vary.

APES: The Living World: Ecosystems::1.3.takeaway: Track the chemical form and process name. Matter moves among reservoirs; one pathway does not imply that every nitrogen atom follows the same sequence.

Psych: Development & Learning::3.4 Class.title: Compare what triggers the same response
Psych: Development & Learning::3.4 Class.prompt: Inspect this fictional classical-conditioning example: a soft light is paired with food that naturally elicits salivation. Predict how the stimulus labels change across phases. The sequence illustrates concepts, not a claim that every pairing always produces learning.

frames.label: Before learning
frames.caption: Food elicits salivation without the relevant pairing history; the light does not yet elicit the target salivation response.

frames.label: Acquisition
frames.caption: The light precedes food on repeated trials. Predictiveness, timing and prior learning can affect acquisition.

stimulus.title: Training trial sequence

steps.title: Soft light appears
steps.text: Initially neutral for this target response.

steps.title: Food follows
steps.text: Unconditioned stimulus.

steps.title: Salivation occurs
steps.text: A response to food; later trials can also include anticipatory responding.

stimulus.note: Pairing describes the training sequence, not a guarantee of an identical outcome in every organism.

frames.label: After learning
frames.caption: In this stated outcome, the light alone now elicits salivation. The light is a conditioned stimulus; salivation to it is a conditioned response.

stimulus.title: Test without food

steps.title: Soft light: conditioned stimulus
steps.text: Presented alone.

steps.title: Salivation: conditioned response
steps.text: Elicited by the learned cue.

steps.title: Food omitted
steps.text: Continued cue-only trials can weaken responding through extinction.

stimulus.note: Extinction is not proof that all prior learning has been erased.

Psych: Development & Learning::3.4 Class.takeaway: Name the response by its eliciting stimulus: salivation to food is unconditioned; salivation to the learned light is conditioned.

Psych: Development & Learning::3.4 Class.title: Which stimulus needed the pairing history?
Psych: Development & Learning::3.4 Class.prompt: These fictional examples concern the stimulus, not the response. Sort each described stimulus using its role in the stated learning sequence.

items.text: A harmless air puff that elicits blinking without the relevant cue-pairing training.
Food that elicits salivation without the relevant cue-pairing training.
A blue light that now elicits anticipatory blinking after repeatedly preceding the air puff.
A short chime that now elicits salivation after repeatedly preceding food.

Psych: Development & Learning::3.4 Class.explanation: The air puff and food elicit the stated responses without this pairing history, making them unconditioned stimuli. The light and chime acquire their response-eliciting roles through the described learning and are conditioned stimuli. Blinking and salivation themselves are responses, not the items being classified.

Psych: Cognition::2.3 Encoding, Storage,.title: Separate processing from later remembering
Psych: Cognition::2.3 Encoding, Storage,.prompt: A fictional learner studies the new word “moraine,” then tries to recall it later. Compare encoding, storage and retrieval. These are interacting processes, not a literal three-box location map of the brain.

frames.label: Encode
frames.caption: The learner connects the word to its meaning and a known example. Encoding concerns how information is initially processed.

stimulus.title: Build a meaningful representation

steps.title: New term
steps.text: “Moraine”

steps.title: Meaning
steps.text: An accumulation of debris transported or deposited by a glacier.

steps.title: Connection
steps.text: Link the term to a previously studied glacier diagram.

stimulus.note: This is an elaborative strategy; it does not guarantee perfect retention.

frames.label: Retain
frames.caption: Storage concerns maintaining information over time. Neither a confident feeling nor an immediate repetition alone establishes durable retention.

stimulus.title: Different questions about the same study event
rows: How was the new word processed?
Is relevant information maintained over time?
Can the learner retrieve it after a delay?

frames.label: Retrieve
frames.caption: A later cue asks for the glacier-debris term. Successful retrieval uses relevant stored information; an unhelpful cue can limit access even when some information remains.

stimulus.title: A later retrieval attempt

steps.title: Cue
steps.text: “What term names this glacier-debris accumulation?”

steps.title: Search / reconstruction
steps.text: Use the meaning and associated diagram.

steps.title: Reported answer
steps.text: “Moraine,” in this stated successful example.

stimulus.note: A failed attempt alone does not identify whether encoding, storage or retrieval was the main problem.

Psych: Cognition::2.3 Encoding, Storage,.takeaway: Encoding is processing, storage is maintenance and retrieval is access. A test response supplies evidence about remembering, but one failure does not locate a unique cause.

Psych: Cognition::2.5 Intelligence, Test.title: Consistency and useful prediction are different checks
Psych: Cognition::2.5 Intelligence, Test.prompt: Inspect four entirely hypothetical paired scores. Compare the repeated test with a separate criterion measure. These tiny teaching datasets are not evidence about a real psychological test or population.

frames.label: Repeated score
frames.caption: The four test–retest pairs fall exactly on y = x, giving r = +1 in this illustrative sample.

frames.label: Different criterion
frames.caption: These four test–criterion pairs have r = 0. The perfect repeat consistency did not establish linear prediction of this criterion.

frames.label: Keep claims separate
frames.caption: The evidence supports different claims. A zero sample correlation does not settle every possible kind of validity or every population.

stimulus.title: What the stated data establish
rows: Perfect consistency in these four pairs
No linear association in these four pairs

Psych: Cognition::2.5 Intelligence, Test.takeaway: Reliability concerns consistency; validity concerns evidence for an intended interpretation and use. One cannot replace the other, and four fictional cases cannot validate a real instrument.

CSP: Algorithms & Programming::3.2 Lists.title: See positions change while values remain recognizable
CSP: Algorithms & Programming::3.2 Lists.prompt: Use AP-style 1-based indexing. Start items = ["map", "rope", "water"]. Execute INSERT(items, 2, "lamp"), then REMOVE(items, 3). Before moving frames, predict which value occupies position 3.

frames.label: Original list
frames.caption: Position 3 initially contains “water.” An index is a current position, not a permanent identifier for that item.

frames.label: After INSERT
frames.caption: Inserting “lamp” at position 2 shifts “rope” to position 3 and “water” to position 4.

frames.label: After REMOVE
frames.caption: REMOVE(items, 3) now deletes “rope,” not the value originally at position 3. “Water” shifts left.

CSP: Algorithms & Programming::3.2 Lists.takeaway: Read each index against the current list. Earlier mutations change which value a later position refers to.

CSP: Data::2.2 Compression and the trade.title: A lossless method can shrink one input and expand another
CSP: Data::2.2 Compression and the trade.prompt: Compare this fully specified teaching encoding. Each run is stored as a 4-bit unsigned count followed by the repeated bit: 5 stored bits per run. Run lengths here are at most 15; ignore other headers. Predict the size before opening the next view.

frames.label: Long runs
frames.caption: The original has 16 bits in two runs. Count 8 is 1000 in binary; the two records are 10000 and 10001.

frames.label: Recover exactly
frames.caption: Decode the count and bit in each record, then concatenate the reconstructed runs. The saved size is 16 − 10 = 6 bits, or 37.5% of the original.

frames.label: Alternating input
frames.caption: For 0101010101010101, every run has count 1. Sixteen 5-bit records use 80 bits: exact recovery still works, but size expands.

CSP: Data::2.2 Compression and the trade.takeaway: Lossless means exact recovery, not guaranteed compression for every input. Count the scheme’s overhead before comparing sizes.

CSP: Computer Systems & Networks::4.1 Th.title: Redundancy can end at a shared bottleneck
CSP: Computer Systems & Networks::4.1 Th.prompt: All shown links are bidirectional. Compare a five-device teaching network as links fail. Predict whether the lab can still reach the destination; removed links are unavailable, not merely slower.

frames.label: All links available
frames.caption: The lab can reach the hub through either North or South, but both routes share Hub–Destination.

stimulus.title: Five devices: two approaches, one final link

frames.label: One route fails
frames.caption: North–Hub is removed. Lab → South → Hub → Destination remains available.

frames.label: Shared link fails
frames.caption: Hub–Destination is also removed. The lab can still reach the hub, but no available link reaches the destination.

CSP: Computer Systems & Networks::4.1 Th.takeaway: Count complete available paths to the destination. Two routes to an intermediate device do not guarantee two independent end-to-end routes.

APUSH: 1844–1877::5.2 Civil War and Eman.title: Freedom: action, policy and constitutional change
APUSH: 1844–1877::5.2 Civil War and Eman.prompt: Move through the frames. What changes at each stage, and what remains unresolved?

frames.label: People act
frames.caption: Historical process: enslaved people shaped wartime circumstances.

stimulus.title: Action changes the wartime problem

steps.title: Enslaved people
steps.text: Escape, resistance and claims to freedom challenge slavery.

steps.title: Union forces
steps.text: Encounters with people seeking freedom create military and political decisions.

steps.title: Policy pressure
steps.text: Actions interact with military needs and abolitionist demands.

stimulus.note: These processes overlap; the arrows show interaction, not one universal personal journey.

frames.label: 1863 policy
frames.caption: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect January 1, 1863.

stimulus.title: Executive wartime action

steps.title: Authority
steps.text: Presidential war powers.

steps.title: Scope
steps.text: Freedom declared for enslaved people in designated rebellious areas; loyal slave states excluded.

steps.title: Implementation
steps.text: Military control and the course of war affect enforcement.

stimulus.note: Limited geographic scope did not make the policy insignificant: it changed the war effort and authorized Black enlistment.

frames.label: 1865 amendment
frames.caption: The Thirteenth Amendment was ratified in December 1865.

stimulus.title: Constitutional abolition

steps.title: Different authority
steps.text: Constitutional amendment, not another executive proclamation.

steps.title: Broader prohibition
steps.text: Slavery and involuntary servitude prohibited, except as punishment for crime after conviction.

steps.title: Remaining struggles
steps.text: Citizenship, voting rights and effective equality require further change.

stimulus.note: Abolition, citizenship and suffrage are distinct legal questions.

APUSH: 1844–1877::5.2 Civil War and Eman.takeaway: Compare authority, scope and implementation. Neither “everyone was immediately free in 1863” nor “the proclamation did nothing” fits the evidence.

APUSH: 1754–1800::3.3 Politics and Power.title: One Constitution, competing interpretations
APUSH: 1754–1800::3.3 Politics and Power.prompt: Compare the bank arguments, then view the institutional outcome.

frames.label: Policy problem
frames.caption: Historical teaching summary: the new government needed workable financial institutions.

stimulus.title: From public credit to a proposal

steps.title: Problem
steps.text: Manage debt and establish federal credit.

steps.title: Hamilton’s proposal
steps.text: A national bank supports fiscal and commercial activity.

steps.title: 1791 decision
steps.text: Congress charters the First Bank of the United States.

stimulus.note: A shared policy problem did not produce agreement about the constitutional solution.

frames.label: Constitutional dispute
frames.caption: These are paraphrased positions, not quotations.

stimulus.title: Two routes through the same dispute

steps.title: Broader construction
steps.text: Supporters connect the bank to enumerated fiscal powers through implied powers.

steps.title: Narrower construction
steps.text: Opponents dispute that the Constitution authorizes this institution.

steps.title: Political stakes
steps.text: Both interpretation and concerns about concentrated financial power matter.

stimulus.note: This comparison does not imply every coalition member held an identical position on every issue.

frames.label: Conflict and continuity
frames.caption: The election of 1800 brought a transfer of presidential power.

stimulus.title: Opposition within a system

steps.title: Disagreement
steps.text: Finance and foreign affairs help organize rival coalitions.

steps.title: Constitutional procedures
steps.text: Election and institutional rules channel the contest.

steps.title: Transfer
steps.text: A rival coalition takes executive office without ending the constitutional system.

stimulus.note: The transfer did not resolve every dispute or establish universal political participation.

APUSH: 1754–1800::3.3 Politics and Power.takeaway: A constitutional framework can persist while its scope and policies remain fiercely contested. Explain the interpretation rather than relying only on party labels.

APUSH: 1865–1898::6.2 Western Expansion.title: Track who controls the land
APUSH: 1865–1898::6.2 Western Expansion.prompt: Each frame changes the question from advertised opportunity to property and sovereignty.

frames.label: Settlement incentive
frames.caption: The Homestead Act was enacted in 1862.

stimulus.title: Opportunity under a federal land policy

steps.title: Federal offer
steps.text: Eligible claimants can seek land under specified conditions.

steps.title: Practical requirements
steps.text: Resources, labor and environmental conditions affect success.

steps.title: Prior claims
steps.text: Indigenous nations already use and govern homelands.

stimulus.note: A federal offer does not establish that land was empty or that all existing claims were respected.

frames.label: Infrastructure and force
frames.caption: Historical mechanisms operated together, with local differences.

stimulus.title: How access becomes control

steps.title: Railroads
steps.text: Transport links encourage migration and commercial production.

steps.title: Federal power
steps.text: Military action and imposed or broken agreements constrain Indigenous autonomy.

steps.title: Changed land use
steps.text: Settlement and extraction redistribute access to resources.

stimulus.note: The arrows describe connected mechanisms, not an identical chronology for every place.

frames.label: 1887 allotment
frames.caption: The Dawes Act was enacted in 1887.

stimulus.title: Change the property rule

steps.title: Collective landholding
steps.text: Reservation lands are targeted for individual allotments.

steps.title: Surplus designation
steps.text: Land classified as surplus becomes available to non-Indigenous acquisition.

steps.title: Consequence
steps.text: Indigenous land loss and weakened collective control follow.

stimulus.note: An assimilationist promise of improvement is a justification to evaluate, not proof of benefit or consent.

APUSH: 1865–1898::6.2 Western Expansion.takeaway: Ask who defines ownership, who can refuse and who gains control. Opportunity for settlers and dispossession of Indigenous peoples can be connected outcomes.

World Hist: Revolutions::5.2 Atlantic re.title: Two dimensions of revolutionary change
World Hist: Revolutions::5.2 Atlantic re.prompt: Compare sovereignty with slavery. Does change in one dimension guarantee change in another?

frames.label: Define the axes
frames.caption: Original comparison framework using historical outcomes.

stimulus.title: Ask two different questions

steps.title: Sovereignty
steps.text: Who exercises political authority over the territory?

steps.title: Slavery
steps.text: Does the political transformation abolish enslavement?

steps.title: Membership
steps.text: Who can exercise rights within the new order?

stimulus.note: These are analytical dimensions, not a numerical ranking of revolutions.

frames.label: American case
frames.caption: Independence was declared in 1776; slavery persisted.

stimulus.title: Independence without general abolition

steps.title: Imperial authority challenged
steps.text: Colonies reject British rule.

steps.title: New political order
steps.text: An independent republic develops.

steps.title: Limit
steps.text: Slavery remains; political participation is restricted.

stimulus.note: Do not infer universal equality from independence or treat the change of sovereignty as insignificant.

frames.label: Haitian case
frames.caption: The revolution began in 1791; Haiti declared independence in 1804.

stimulus.title: Abolition and independence

steps.title: Enslaved people act
steps.text: Revolt challenges slavery and colonial power.

steps.title: Contested struggle
steps.text: Shifting coalitions and imperial conflicts shape the revolution.

steps.title: Outcome
steps.text: An independent Haiti emerges from the destruction of slavery.

stimulus.note: The comparison concerns specific outcomes; it does not erase conflict within either revolution.

World Hist: Revolutions::5.2 Atlantic re.takeaway: A defensible comparison specifies the institution changed. Independence, abolition and equal political membership are related but distinct.

World Hist: Consequences of Industrializ.title: Motive, capacity, justification, effect
World Hist: Consequences of Industrializ.prompt: Change frames to see why these four categories should not be collapsed.

frames.label: Why and how
frames.caption: Historical analytical model, not a single event.

stimulus.title: Separate objective from means

steps.title: Motive
steps.text: Strategic position, resources, markets or prestige.

steps.title: Capacity
steps.text: Transport, weapons, finance, administration and alliances.

steps.title: Decision
steps.text: Actors use available means to pursue a particular objective.

stimulus.note: A technology can enable expansion without explaining why a specific territory was targeted.

frames.label: Claim and institution
frames.caption: Constructed port-concession example; not a named historical treaty.

stimulus.title: Test the public defense

steps.title: Justification
steps.text: A state calls its demanded concession progress.

steps.title: Institution
steps.text: The concession transfers customs control under threatened force.

steps.title: Question
steps.text: Who can meaningfully refuse, collect revenue or set the rules?

stimulus.note: The model’s words are original teaching material, not historical quotations.

frames.label: Evaluate effects
frames.caption: The same constructed example, now viewed from affected groups.

stimulus.title: Do not let a slogan stand in for evidence

steps.title: State and company
steps.text: Seek strategy and fee revenue.

steps.title: Local authority
steps.text: Loses control over customs decisions.

steps.title: Further evidence needed
steps.text: Terms, enforcement and distribution determine consequences for residents.

stimulus.note: A transfer of control does not establish that every resident had the same experience.

World Hist: Consequences of Industrializ.takeaway: Motive explains an objective; capacity explains a means; justification claims legitimacy. Evaluate actual control and consequences separately.

World Hist: Land-Based Empires::3.2 Reli.title: A monument makes a claim. Who accepts it?
World Hist: Land-Based Empires::3.2 Reli.prompt: Compare three sources about one constructed royal project.

frames.label: Court image
frames.caption: Original source model, not a surviving historical object.

stimulus.title: Representation

steps.title: Commission
steps.text: A court funds an image of the ruler.

steps.title: Symbols
steps.text: Sacred duty and dynastic ancestors appear beside the ruler.

steps.title: Inference
steps.text: The court presents authority as rightful and continuous.

stimulus.note: The image reveals an intended representation, not every subject’s private belief.

frames.label: Account book
frames.caption: Original source model for the same project.

stimulus.title: Production

steps.title: Record
steps.text: Payments go to builders and craftspeople.

steps.title: Inference
steps.text: Resources and organized labor support the monument.

steps.title: Limit
steps.text: The account may omit unpaid burdens or other costs.

stimulus.note: Material grandeur depends on production; it does not prove universal approval.

frames.label: Local petition
frames.caption: Original source model for the same project.

stimulus.title: Contested burden

steps.title: Complaint
steps.text: A community objects to labor demands.

steps.title: Inference
steps.text: Some subjects challenge the project’s costs.

steps.title: Limit
steps.text: One petition does not establish every community’s response.

stimulus.note: Representation, production and reception are different questions answered by different evidence.

World Hist: Land-Based Empires::3.2 Reli.takeaway: Use each source for what it can establish. A powerful public image can coexist with unequal burdens and resistance.

US Gov: Civil Liberties & Civil Rights::.title: Three gates in a rights analysis
US Gov: Civil Liberties & Civil Rights::.prompt: Move from the government actor to the right, then to the action. Do not skip a gate.

frames.label: Original reach
frames.caption: Barron v. Baltimore (1833) confirmed the Bill of Rights did not directly bind states.

stimulus.title: First identify the actor

steps.title: Actor
steps.text: Is the challenged action federal, state, local or private?

steps.title: Original framework
steps.text: The Bill of Rights initially constrained the federal government.

steps.title: Problem
steps.text: A state action requires a state-applicability analysis.

stimulus.note: Private action raises a separate state-action question; not every private dispute is a constitutional violation.

frames.label: State applicability
frames.caption: The Fourteenth Amendment was ratified in 1868.

stimulus.title: Then identify the particular protection

steps.title: Constitutional route
steps.text: The Court uses the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause for selective incorporation.

steps.title: Specific right
steps.text: Ask whether this protection applies against state and local government.

steps.title: Examples
steps.text: Gideon (1963): appointed counsel in state felony prosecutions. McDonald (2010): Second Amendment incorporation.

stimulus.note: Incorporation developed protection by protection; it was not all completed in 1868.

frames.label: Violation question
frames.caption: Original hypothetical: a state defendant requests appointed counsel in a felony prosecution.

stimulus.title: Applicability is not the final answer

steps.title: Right applies
steps.text: The state is bound by the incorporated protection.

steps.title: Relevant facts
steps.text: Examine inability to afford counsel and the proceeding at issue.

steps.title: Legal evaluation
steps.text: Apply the governing rule to determine whether the action violates the protection.

stimulus.note: A protection’s applicability and a particular violation are distinct conclusions.

US Gov: Civil Liberties & Civil Rights::.takeaway: Actor → specific right and state applicability → facts and rule. Incorporation does not mean every government action automatically violates a right.

US Gov: Interactions Among Branches::2.1.title: Where does administrative choice enter?
US Gov: Interactions Among Branches::2.1.prompt: Follow an original hypothetical statute through implementation and oversight.

frames.label: Congress authorizes
frames.caption: Constructed example, not an actual statute.

stimulus.title: Legislative boundary

steps.title: Statute
steps.text: Congress directs an agency to regulate a specified pollutant.

steps.title: Delegation
steps.text: The law authorizes implementation within stated goals and limits.

steps.title: Open details
steps.text: Measurement and inspection procedures require further decisions.

stimulus.note: Delegation is not unlimited authority to pursue any policy the agency prefers.

frames.label: Agency chooses
frames.caption: The same hypothetical example.

stimulus.title: Discretion within the assignment

steps.title: Technical choice
steps.text: Select an authorized measurement procedure.

steps.title: Rulemaking
steps.text: Use applicable procedures, including notice and comment when required.

steps.title: Implementation
steps.text: Publish and administer the resulting requirements.

stimulus.note: Public comments inform the process; the most comments do not automatically win as in an election.

frames.label: Choices remain bounded
frames.caption: Oversight routes can interact; this is not a required chronological sequence.

stimulus.title: Review and accountability

steps.title: Congress
steps.text: Oversight, funding choices and statutory revision.

steps.title: Executive branch
steps.text: Supervision within legal authority.

steps.title: Courts
steps.text: Review legal challenges under governing law.

stimulus.note: A challenge or disagreement does not automatically invalidate a rule. The legal basis and procedures matter.

US Gov: Interactions Among Branches::2.1.takeaway: Discretion fills authorized gaps; oversight tests boundaries. Distinguish the statute, the agency’s implementation choice and the review of that choice.

AP Lang: Positions, Sources, and Synthes.title: Turn three source notes into one argument
AP Lang: Positions, Sources, and Synthes.prompt: Compare isolated summaries, relationships and a qualified claim.

frames.label: Read each contribution
frames.caption: Complete original hypothetical source set about a museum program.

stimulus.title: Keep the source roles distinct

steps.title: A: visitor
steps.text: Weekday work prevents my visit; Saturday would give me an option.

steps.title: B: operations
steps.text: Saturday opening requires staffing beyond the current plan.

steps.title: C: proposal
steps.text: Try one Saturday and record attendance and staffing needs.

stimulus.note: These are constructed sources, not real research. A reports one person’s availability, not schoolwide or townwide demand.

frames.label: Find the relationship
frames.caption: The sources answer different parts of the decision.

stimulus.title: Not every difference is a contradiction

steps.title: A contributes
steps.text: A possible access benefit.

steps.title: B qualifies
steps.text: An operational condition.

steps.title: C responds
steps.text: A bounded way to investigate benefit and feasibility.

stimulus.note: A and B can both be true; preference and staffing are not incompatible factual claims.

frames.label: Build your position
frames.caption: Original model claim, not a guaranteed outcome.

stimulus.title: Synthesis has a direction

steps.title: Claim
steps.text: Consider a limited Saturday trial.

steps.title: Condition
steps.text: Evaluate attendance and staffing before expansion.

steps.title: Reasoning
steps.text: Test the possible benefit while addressing the documented constraint.

stimulus.note: Follow the actual assignment’s source requirements. This three-source mini-model is not a full exam source packet.

AP Lang: Positions, Sources, and Synthes.takeaway: Organize sources by the question they help answer. Synthesis is the relationship you explain, not a list of source summaries.

AP Lang: Rhetorical Situation and Purpos.title: From topic to defensible analysis
AP Lang: Rhetorical Situation and Purpos.prompt: See what each revision adds to the same original editorial.

frames.label: Read the evidence
frames.caption: Original miniature editorial to families.

stimulus.title: A complete source to inspect

steps.title: Schedule
steps.text: “The club ends at five; the last bus leaves at four.”

steps.title: Consequence
steps.text: “Participation should not depend on a parent leaving work.”

steps.title: Request
steps.text: “Ask the board to try one late route.”

stimulus.note: All quoted wording is original instructional writing, not an attributed real editorial.

frames.label: Name the claim type
frames.caption: Compare statements about this source.

stimulus.title: Topic is not analysis

steps.title: Topic
steps.text: School transportation.

steps.title: Observation
steps.text: The writer gives two times.

steps.title: Policy opinion
steps.text: The school should add a late bus.

stimulus.note: An observation may be accurate and a policy opinion defensible, but neither yet explains how the editorial works.

frames.label: Make an analytical thesis
frames.caption: Original model interpretation.

stimulus.title: Choice → audience concern → purpose

steps.title: Choice
steps.text: Contrasts club and bus schedules.

steps.title: Concern
steps.text: Frames participation as a family access burden.

steps.title: Thesis direction
steps.text: Uses that mismatch to support a limited late-route request.

stimulus.note: This explains a plausible strategy, not proof that every family was persuaded.

AP Lang: Rhetorical Situation and Purpos.takeaway: A defensible analytical thesis interprets specific choices in relation to audience and purpose. It does not merely name the issue or agree with the policy.

Standard English Conventions::Sentence B.title: Build a legal sentence boundary
Standard English Conventions::Sentence B.prompt: Original examples: inspect the clauses before choosing punctuation.

frames.label: Find the clauses
frames.caption: Both groups can stand alone.

stimulus.title: Two independent clauses

steps.title: Clause 1
steps.text: The archive opened early.

steps.title: Clause 2
steps.text: The researchers entered.

steps.title: Diagnosis
steps.text: A comma alone cannot join these independent clauses.

stimulus.note: “The archive opened early, the researchers entered” is a comma splice in standard written English.

frames.label: Choose a legal join
frames.caption: Each example preserves two independent clauses.

stimulus.title: Three valid structures

steps.title: Period
steps.text: The archive opened early. The researchers entered.

steps.title: Semicolon
steps.text: The archive opened early; the researchers entered.

steps.title: Comma + coordinator
steps.text: The archive opened early, and the researchers entered.

stimulus.note: The alternatives are not interchangeable in every question: preserve intended meaning and surrounding grammar.

frames.label: Change the structure
frames.caption: One clause now depends on the other.

stimulus.title: Subordination changes the test

steps.title: Dependent opening
steps.text: Because the archive opened early,

steps.title: Independent clause
steps.text: the researchers entered before noon.

steps.title: Complete sentence
steps.text: The dependent clause attaches to a complete main clause.

stimulus.note: “Because the archive opened early” alone is a fragment in this ordinary prose context. Because also asserts a causal relationship.

Standard English Conventions::Sentence B.takeaway: Identify independent and dependent clauses first. Punctuation must fit the structure; a pause in your reading is not enough.

Expression of Ideas::Transitions.title: The relationship comes before the transition
Expression of Ideas::Transitions.prompt: Compare three original pairs about a study room. Similar topics can require different links.

frames.label: Contrast
frames.caption: Sentence 2 limits an expectation raised by sentence 1.

stimulus.title: Difference or qualification

steps.title: Idea 1
steps.text: The room gained more seats.

steps.title: Idea 2
steps.text: Its opening hours did not change.

steps.title: Signal
steps.text: However can mark this contrast.

stimulus.note: The contrast concerns capacity versus time; do not infer that either change caused the other.

frames.label: Consequence
frames.caption: The connection is supplied in the example.

stimulus.title: A result follows a stated condition

steps.title: Idea 1
steps.text: The room is closed during the repair.

steps.title: Idea 2
steps.text: Students must use another location during that closure.

steps.title: Signal
steps.text: Therefore can mark this consequence.

stimulus.note: A consequence transition asserts a logical connection; it cannot manufacture one from unrelated facts.

frames.label: Illustration
frames.caption: Sentence 2 gives a particular case of the first claim.

stimulus.title: General point → specific instance

steps.title: Idea 1
steps.text: The room supports several study activities.

steps.title: Idea 2
steps.text: Students can rehearse presentations there.

steps.title: Signal
steps.text: For example introduces the specific activity.

stimulus.note: Read enough context to determine the relationship, not only the transition word or a repeated topic.

Expression of Ideas::Transitions.takeaway: Paraphrase the relationship first: contrast, consequence or illustration. Then choose the transition that accurately signals it.

Calc AB: Contextual Applications of Diff.title: Is speed increasing or decreasing?
Calc AB: Contextual Applications of Diff.prompt: The values refer to one instant of one-dimensional motion. Velocity v is in meters/second and acceleration a in meters/second². No velocity is zero. Sort by whether |v| is increasing or decreasing at that instant.
Calc AB: Contextual Applications of Diff.explanation: For nonzero velocity, speed increases when v and a have the same sign and decreases when their signs differ. Negative acceleration alone does not mean slowing down: with negative velocity it makes the velocity more negative and its magnitude larger. The zero-velocity case was excluded because it requires separate local analysis.

Stats: Probability, Random Variables, an.title: Does one event change the other’s probability?
Stats: Probability, Random Variables, an.prompt: Every card fully specifies its hypothetical random process and events A and B. Sort the event pair as independent or dependent; independence means P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), not that the events cannot occur together.

items.text: Two independent fair coin tosses: A = first is heads; B = second is heads.
Draw uniformly twice, with replacement and remixing, from 2 red and 2 blue tokens: A = first red; B = second red.
One fair six-sided die: A = even; B = greater than 3.
Draw one card uniformly from {R1,R2,B1,B2}: A = red; B = blue.

Stats: Probability, Random Variables, an.explanation: The independent coin tosses have joint probability 1/4=(1/2)(1/2). Replacement and remixing preserve a 1/2 red probability on both token draws, also giving joint 1/4. For the die, A∩B={4,6} has probability 1/3, unlike (1/2)(1/2)=1/4. For the single card, red and blue are disjoint positive-probability events: joint probability 0 differs from 1/4, so they are dependent.

Physics 1: Work, Energy, and Power::3.1.title: Which way does this force transfer energy?
Physics 1: Work, Energy, and Power::3.1.prompt: Sort the work done by the stated constant force. Each displacement is horizontal; consider only that named force, not net work. None of these forces is perpendicular to the displacement.

items.text: A 15 N push points right while the object moves 2 m right.
A 10 N resistive force points left while the object moves 3 m right.
An 8 N pull points left while the object moves 1 m left.
A 5 N pull points right while the object moves 4 m left.

Physics 1: Work, Energy, and Power::3.1.explanation: A force component along displacement does positive work; a component opposite displacement does negative work. The four works, in item order, are +30 J, −30 J, +8 J and −20 J. Leftward is not automatically negative work: the force and displacement directions must be compared.

APES: Atmospheric Pollution::7.1 Primary.title: Emitted directly or formed afterward?
APES: Atmospheric Pollution::7.1 Primary.prompt: Sort each pollutant by the process explicitly described. Primary and secondary refer to its origin in this scenario, not how dangerous or concentrated it is.

items.text: Carbon monoxide released directly from a vehicle exhaust.
Sulfur dioxide released directly by burning sulfur-containing fuel.
Ground-level ozone formed through sunlight-driven reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds.
Sulfuric acid formed in the atmosphere through oxidation of sulfur dioxide and reactions involving water.

APES: Atmospheric Pollution::7.1 Primary.explanation: The stated CO and SO₂ enter the air directly and are primary pollutants. The stated ozone and sulfuric acid form through atmospheric reactions and are secondary pollutants. A precursor can be primary while the substance formed from it is secondary.

Psych: Development & Learning::3.5 Opera.title: Did the behavior become more or less frequent?
Psych: Development & Learning::3.5 Opera.prompt: Sort the consequence by its observed effect on the specified behavior in these fictional cases. Reinforcement and punishment are defined by behavior change, not whether a consequence sounds pleasant.

items.text: Submitting a practice log earns a token; afterward the learner submits logs more often.
Checking an equipment setting stops an irritating alert; afterward the worker checks the setting more often.
Posting off-topic messages leads to temporary loss of forum privileges; afterward off-topic posting decreases.
Skipping a routine check leads to an extra corrective form; afterward skipping checks decreases.

Psych: Development & Learning::3.5 Opera.explanation: The first two consequences increase the target behavior, so both are reinforcement; the alert stopping illustrates removal of an aversive condition. The last two decrease the target behavior, so both are punishment. Adding versus removing a consequence is a separate distinction from increasing versus decreasing behavior.

CSP: Impact of Computing::5.2 Personal d.title: Identity check or permission check?
CSP: Impact of Computing::5.2 Personal d.prompt: Sort each system operation by the question it answers. Assume the operations work as stated; this activity distinguishes their roles rather than claiming that any one check makes a system completely secure.

items.text: A service verifies the submitted password for the account being claimed.
A service verifies a registered security device as an additional identity factor.
After sign-in, the server checks whether this account may open the requested private report.
Before allowing a course edit, the server checks whether this signed-in account has the instructor role.

CSP: Impact of Computing::5.2 Personal d.explanation: Authentication checks who the user claims to be; authorization checks what that identified user is permitted to do. A successful password or device check does not automatically authorize access to every report or editing action.
